title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 132
paragraphs: Of all days, their custom is to honor most the day on which each one was born: on this day they think it right to set out a more lavish feast than on other days. At this feast, the wealthier among them set upon the table an ox, a horse, a camel, or an ass, roasted whole in an oven; the poor set out small animals in the same way. They have few solid dishes, but many served afterwards as dessert, and these not in a single course. For this reason the Persians say that the Hellenes leave off dinner hungry, because after dinner they have nothing worth mentioning served as dessert; whereas, if any good dessert were served up, they would not stop eating so soon. They are very much given to wine-drinking, and it is not permitted for a man to vomit or to make water in the presence of another. So they guard against these things. They are also accustomed to deliberate over matters of the greatest importance when they are drinking hard, and whatever conclusion has pleased them in their deliberation, this on the next day, when they are sober, the master of the house in which they happen to be when deliberating lays before them again for discussion. If it pleases them when sober as well, they adopt it; but if it does not please them, they let it go. And whatever they have first deliberated on when sober, they reconsider when they are drinking.
